articleTitle: CCSDS recommendation on lossless data compression: the ESA contribution
publicationTitle: IEE 5th CCSDS Workshop New Technologies, New Standards (Ref. No. 1998/519)
abstract: Every year, due to more sophisticated sensors and more powerful high data rate instruments, the data collected by new satellites is constantly growing and leading to higher and higher downlink bandwidth demand. As it is not foreseeable an increase in the downlink bandwidth allocation (both for infrastructure reasons and spectrum allocation), satellites have to improve on-board data reduction and data encoding techniques. A lossless compression technique guarantees full reconstruction of the original data without incurring any data distortion and is particularly useful when data integrity cannot be compromised. In the decompression processes the original data are reconstructed by restoring the redundancy removed during the compression phase. The Consultative Committee for Space Data Systems (CCSDS) has recently issued a Recommendation for lossless data compression selecting the Rice algorithm as lossless data compression algorithm. The paper reports on the ESA contribution to CCSDS lossless data compression by presenting the activities and products performed both at ESTEC and ESOC. It deals first with the software model of Rice algorithm, which has been developed, internally at ESTEC. Then it presents the ongoing hardware implementation (ASIC) of the Rice algorithm. Such an ASIC is able to interface the virtual channel assembler and the virtual channel multiplexer components, well known by spacecraft designers and implementers. Finally the strategy adopted in the design of the CCSDS-Rice decompression software library to produce a flexible and efficient decompression tool for packetized and "raw" compressed data is presented.

articleTitle: CCSDS telemetry channel coding: the turbo coding option
publicationTitle: IEE 5th CCSDS Workshop New Technologies, New Standards (Ref. No. 1998/519)
abstract: As of 1993 a new coding concept promising gains as close as 0.5 dB to the Shannon limit on bit error rates was introduced by Berrou et al. The coding scheme called turbo coding achieved immediate worldwide attention. After the first discussions in the May '96 Meeting of the Consultative Committee for Space Data Systems (CCSDS), it was decided-in agreement with NASA and other national space agencies-to include a set of turbo codes in a new issue of the CCSDS telemetry channel coding recommendation. Turbo coding will be an add-on option to the recommendations without modifying the existing coding schemes and will retain compatibility with the CCSDS Packet Telemetry recommendation. Pink sheets updating the recommendation are currently being reviewed to formally establish turbo coding as an alternative to both Reed-Solomon and convolutional coding for deep space and near-Earth missions. This paper presents the turbo codes that are being proposed for the recommendation, and their expected higher coding gain with respect to the present encoding schemes.

articleTitle: A component architecture for platform-independent space link extension services
publicationTitle: IEE 5th CCSDS Workshop New Technologies, New Standards (Ref. No. 1998/519)
abstract: We are proposing a novel method of specifying and implementing CCSDS Space Link Extension (SLE) services. Traditionally, such services would be functionally specified (perhaps via an Application Programming Interface, or API) and accessed via a "wire protocol" implemented on a physical network (e.g., TCP/IP over Ethernet). Specification of such a service interface at the "wire level" typically is used to guarantee interoperability between separate implementations (e.g., between both sides of an interface agreement). However, when issues such as security are considered (some of which have not yet been adequately addressed), such a wire-level specification is likely to severely limit future implementations and capabilities of the SLE services. We are therefore proposing a novel layered architecture for the SLE services, which frees each party from having to interoperate at the wire level. Our approach thus specifies the SLE services as a set of software components that communicate with each other using standard invocation methods implemented on every computer (e.g., "subroutine call"). This "component approach" has many benefits, such as: a) separates API specification from implementation issues; b) allows modular deployment of service components; c) leverages recent advances in software development methodology; d) facilitates operation over standards-based infrastructure; e) frees application from knowledge of lower layers; f) allows applications and services to utilize modules dynamically; g) requires no use of vendor-specific tools or infrastructure. Further, we do not rely upon any vendor-specific tools or infrastructure, and have constructed the API to allow implementation either synchronously or asynchronously, with or without the use of threading.

publicationTitle: IEE 5th CCSDS Workshop New Technologies, New Standards (Ref. No. 1998/519)
abstract: The Rosetta mission is a cometary mission, which will be launched in 2003 by Ariane 5. After a long cruise phase, the satellite will rendezvous with Comet Wirtanen and orbit it, while taking scientific measurements. A Surface Science Package (SSP) will be landed on the comet surface to take in-situ measurements. During the cruise phase, the satellite will be given gravity assist manoeuvres once by Mars and twice by the Earth. The satellite will also take measurements in the fly-bys of two asteroids. The Rosetta mission has characteristics differing quite considerably from those deep space missions hitherto supported at ESOC. One of these is the use of packet telemetry and packet telecommanding. Rosetta is the first ESA deep space mission using these standards. This paper describes in detail how the Rosetta on-board and ground segment design uses packetised telemetry and commands taking into account the deep space characteristic of the Rosetta mission. In particular the paper describes how Rosetta is designed to overcome two major problems with deep space missions, the relative low downlink rate and the long turnaround time for telecommands.

publicationTitle: IEE 5th CCSDS Workshop New Technologies, New Standards (Ref. No. 1998/519)
abstract: ESA is developing space qualified data compression chips using a compression algorithm suitable for most future missions. This so-called quasi-lossless compressor has the following characteristics: 1) cover the whole range from truly lossless compression to lossy compression with high compression ratio; 2) uses sub-band coding techniques to allow progressive transmission of images from low to high resolution; 3) uses digital wavelet transform decorrelation, quantization, embedded zero-tree coder and entropy coder, which allows modular architecture. This concept has been submitted for CCSDS standardisation. The status of the lossless compressor chip or PRDC (packetizing Rice data compressor) ASIC development is also presented.

publicationTitle: IEE 5th CCSDS Workshop New Technologies, New Standards (Ref. No. 1998/519)
abstract: To date, many civil space missions have relied on the unique nature of space mission data systems to prevent unauthorised access to ground and space assets. However, within the relatively open environment created by the use of space data system standards, it is now essential that the security requirements for space missions are given priority. Specific security measures will be required within the space mission data system to counter specific threats from a wide range of sources. This has always been the case for military space missions, but as civil space systems start to play a role within safety-of-life applications such as air traffic control, the requirements for security are becoming increasingly important. Also, many civil missions now have important commercial interests which require protection. Work has commenced within the Consultative Committee for Space Data Systems (CCSDS) to develop an approach for applying security to CCSDS protocols. This paper introduces the different security threats and requirements that should be considered for the various space mission types as well as the technical approaches and mechanisms that can be used to counter specific threats. In the concert of space mission operations, encryption, authentication and data integrity mechanisms are reviewed. This examination is carried out with reference to the security architecture that has been developed by ISO and is used to present a potential CCSDS Security Architecture.

publicationTitle: IEE 5th CCSDS Workshop New Technologies, New Standards (Ref. No. 1998/519)
abstract: The CEO Programme is a European Community funded programme for advancing the use of Earth Observation (EO) data. As part of this programme CEO is developing INFEO, an interoperable catalogue system that allows simultaneous searching of major EO data collections distributed all over the world. INFEO is based on CIP (Catalogue Interoperability Protocol), which is an application profile of the existing search and retrieval protocol 239.50 aimed specifically at EO datasets. CIP was designed by CEOS, whose members-all the world's civil agencies involved in EO satellite programmes-will use it to give access to their catalogues. An advantage of CIP is that it covers all catalogue services like Search, Browse, Retrieve, and Order, which allows the use of one tool to get or give access to all services. Furthermore, CIP supports catalogue specifics so that all catalogue information can be made available, and CIP has self-describing metadata, which helps to keep information up-to-date. Last but not least CIP has collections, a mechanism to organise data in a hierarchical structure. Through collections the data can be viewed in themes, which makes finding suitable data products both easier and more efficient.

publicationTitle: IEE 5th CCSDS Workshop New Technologies, New Standards (Ref. No. 1998/519)
abstract: Standards have been under development through the Consultative Committee for Space Data Systems for several years and, in common with other international standards, equipment software and systems are being produced conforming to them. In the field of telecommunications, Type Approval is the means by which equipment from diverse manufacturers is confirmed as conforming to the appropriate standards, poses no threat to network integrity and (especially in the case of satellite communication systems and other wireless networks) will not interfere with other networks. In other words, the interoperability defined by conformance to the standards is assured by requiring equipment to have undergone Type Approval testing prior to any attempt to interconnect with a network. Type Approval requirements and procedures exist for numerous systems and networks, including GSM cellular telephony and satellite communications, as well as for telephone modems and fax machines. This paper concentrates on satellite communications.
